newsitem.title: USA: Lawmakers call for removal of US farm tax threat.
newsitem.headline: Lawmakers call for removal of US farm tax threat.

text.p: Farm-state lawmakers pledged Thursday to press for speedy passage of bills exempting "forward contracts," a merchandising tool that is widely used by farmers, from being subject to the alternative minimum tax.
The legislation was spawned by concern in farm country of potentially huge tax bills. Forward contracts allow farmers to defer income on sale of their crops into the next tax year.
"This is a huge issue in my district," said Representative Tom Latham, Iowa Republican.
Bills to create the exemption were filed in the House and Senate. Sponsors said they would fight for passage soon.

Washington Republican Rep. Jennifer Dunn, a member of the Ways and Means Committee, said she would try to include the exemption in "the first available tax act" or to approve it as a noncontroversial "technical correction."
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said last month that he would support efforts to rewrite the law.

Farmers are concerned by a recent Internal Revenue Service decision involving a potato farmer who had to pay the alternative minimum tax. The IRS ruled that income had to be counted in the year the forward contract was signed, not the year the money was received.

"People are very concerned about this situation out there and they should be," said Nebraska Republican Rep. Bill Barrett. He said one farmer, with an income of $30,000, would face a tax bill of $32,000 instead of $6,000 if a forward contract for $100,000 was deemed liable this year.
Rep. George Nethercutt, Washington Republican, the House sponsor of the bill, said he and his 68 cosponsors believed the bill "will pass early and properly."
"All of us will pull together to try to get this through quickly," said Minnesota Democrat Rep. David Minge.
